questions: Which API Connect deployment profile style provides high availability for production in CP4I?
A three-replica profile (for example n3xc4.m16-style profiles) that runs subsystem components with three replicas
Any profile, because HA is automatic
API Connect profiles encode replica count and size. 'n3' profiles deploy three replicas for HA, while 'n1' profiles suit non-production.
Wrong: HA depends on the profile.
Production uses an n3 profile, and dev uses n1 to save resources.
Profile naming: nX = replicas, cY = CPU, mZ = memory.
Why do three-replica API Connect management and portal components need three or more worker nodes, ideally in separate zones?
So that replicas (including database and quorum-based components) are spread across failure domains and survive a node or zone loss while keeping quorum
Because each replica needs a dedicated license
Because the portal requires RWX storage
Because the gateway cannot run with the manager
HA requires replicas on independent failure domains. Quorum-based components need a majority surviving.
Management database replicas run in zones a, b and c; a zone loss leaves 2 of 3.
Three replicas on one node = no real HA.
The API Connect management subsystem is degraded after a node failure, and one database replica is not ready. API Manager still works. What does this indicate?
The remaining replicas still form a working quorum (degraded HA), so the failed replica should be recovered promptly to restore full redundancy
API Connect requires a full reinstall
With 3 replicas, losing one keeps the service available but with no remaining fault tolerance. Recovering the replica restores full HA.
Wrong: data persists in the surviving replicas.
Once the node was restored, the database replica re-synced and status returned to Ready.
Degraded = one more failure away from an outage. Act quickly.
How does the API gateway continue serving existing APIs if the API Connect management subsystem is temporarily unavailable?
Gateways hold the configuration (APIs, products, subscriptions) already pushed to them, so runtime calls continue; only management operations such as publishing or new subscriptions are affected
The gateway queries management on every call
The management plane pushes configuration to gateways, which enforce it locally. A management outage affects changes but not existing traffic.
Correct: the data plane is independent of the control plane at runtime.
During a management upgrade, partner API traffic continued without interruption.
Control plane outage does not mean a data plane outage. Know the difference.
A company needs its API runtime to survive a regional outage with RTO under 5 minutes, while API management changes can tolerate several hours of RTO. Which design is MOST cost-effective?

Active gateways in both regions serving traffic behind a GSLB, with management (and portal) in active/passive 2DCDR or restored from backup within hours; gateways keep enforcing the last-known configuration
Active/active management across regions with synchronous replication
A single region with backups for everything
DNS pointing only to region A, with manual reconfiguration of gateways after failure
Separating data plane and control plane objectives allows a cheaper design: runtime availability is met by multi-region gateways, while management uses a less expensive DR approach.
Correct: tiered control and data plane DR.
Wrong: not supported this way, and costly.
Gateways in EU and US both serve api.example.com; the management passive site is promoted only if the EU region is lost for more than 1 hour.
Separate RTOs for runtime and management lead to cheaper, smarter DR.
Which is a key advantage of Native HA over multi-instance queue managers in Kubernetes?
Native HA does not require shared RWX file storage with special locking; each replica uses its own RWO block volume and MQ replicates the data
Native HA allows three active instances
Native HA needs no persistent storage
Native HA removes the dependency on a shared file system that meets MQ's locking requirements, which is often hard to provide reliably in cloud environments.
Correct: no shared file system dependency.
In a public cloud with only zonal block volumes, Native HA is the natural choice.
A multi-instance queue manager fails over, but the standby cannot start and logs file-locking errors. What is the MOST likely cause?
The shared file system does not release or honour locks correctly (for example NFS lease or locking misconfiguration)
The queue manager has too many channels
Multi-instance depends on file locks to coordinate active and standby. Locking issues prevent takeover or risk corruption.
amqmfsck testing revealed the NFS server's lock lease issues.
Multi-instance problems -> check the shared file system first.
What happens to messages on a queue manager that fails in an MQ cluster with no HA configured for that queue manager?
They are unavailable until that queue manager is recovered, because MQ clusters do not replicate messages
They are automatically moved to another cluster member
MQ clustering does not replicate messages. Messages on a failed member are stranded until it recovers, which is why each member needs its own HA.
Wrong: persistent messages are recovered when it restarts.
Each uniform cluster member runs as Native HA, so stranding is limited to seconds.
MQ cluster + Native HA = scale + availability.
An architect combines a uniform cluster of three queue managers with Native HA for each. What does each layer provide?
The uniform cluster provides horizontal scale and application rebalancing across queue managers; Native HA provides fast failover of each queue manager so its messages are not stranded
The uniform cluster replicates messages; Native HA balances load
Combining them gives scalability (more queue managers with balanced applications) and availability (each queue manager recovers quickly).
Nine pods total: three queue managers x three Native HA replicas, with applications spread across the three active instances.
Which TWO settings help Event Streams keep accepting writes during a single broker failure while avoiding data loss? (Select TWO.)

With replication factor 3, each partition has three copies. min.insync.replicas=2 requires at least two in-sync copies before an acks=all write is acknowledged. If one broker fails, two replicas remain in sync, so writes continue and every acknowledged record exists on at least two brokers. RF=1 or acks=0 give up that protection.
Correct: durability threshold plus producer acknowledgement.
Broker 2 is drained for patching; producers continue with no errors.
RF 3 / min ISR 2 / acks=all: memorize it.
After a broker restart, all partition leaders remain on two of three brokers, which overloads them. What should be done?
Trigger preferred leader election (or rely on auto leader rebalancing) and, if needed, a Cruise Control rebalance to spread leadership and load
After restarts, leadership may not return to preferred replicas automatically. Preferred leader election rebalances leadership; Cruise Control can rebalance replicas too.
Running preferred leader election restored an even spread of leaders and halved the CPU on the hot brokers.
Uneven leadership causes hot brokers. Rebalance.
How should Kafka consumers be designed to tolerate broker failovers and rebalances gracefully?
Commit offsets after processing, make processing idempotent, handle rebalance callbacks (commit or cleanup on revoke), and use cooperative rebalancing where supported
Commit offsets before processing and ignore rebalances
Use one consumer per topic only
Robust consumers process at least once with idempotency, manage commits around rebalances, and minimize stop-the-world rebalances.
Wrong: risks data loss on failure.
Switching to the cooperative-sticky assignor cut rebalance pauses from 30 seconds to under 2.
Rebalances are normal. Design consumers for them.
Consumers in a group frequently rebalance, and logs show 'member left group due to poll timeout'. What is the cause?
Processing between poll() calls exceeds max.poll.interval.ms, so the consumer is considered failed
The topic has too many partitions
If a consumer does not poll within max.poll.interval.ms, it is removed from the group, which triggers rebalances. Reduce batch size (max.poll.records), speed up processing, or increase the interval.
Lowering max.poll.records from 500 to 50 stopped the rebalances.
Poll timeout -> processing too slow per batch.
An ACE runtime scaled to 6 replicas, but throughput did not improve. The flow is MQ-driven, and the queue manager CPU is at 100%. What is the bottleneck?
The queue manager, not ACE; scale or tune MQ (for example add queue managers, increase resources, or optimize persistence) because more consumers cannot exceed its capacity
Scaling consumers does not help if the shared dependency is saturated. Identify the actual bottleneck before scaling.
Correct: the dependency is the bottleneck.
Moving to a larger queue manager CPU limit and splitting queues across two queue managers doubled throughput.
Scale the bottleneck, not the most convenient component.
What is the effect of 'additional instances' on an ACE message flow?
It adds threads within the integration server to process messages concurrently for that flow

In ACE, additional instances adds threads to a message flow inside one integration server, so it processes more messages concurrently in that pod. Replicas add pods. Total concurrency is roughly (1 + additional instances) x replicas, and this also multiplies connections to downstream systems such as databases and queue managers.
additionalInstances=4 lets a flow process 5 messages concurrently per pod.
A REST API implemented in ACE has spiky traffic: 50 requests per second normally and 2,000 for 10 minutes during flash sales. Which design is MOST appropriate?

Rate-limit at the API gateway to protect back ends, autoscale ACE replicas with sufficient minimum replicas (pre-scaled before known events), ensure cluster autoscaling or capacity headroom, and use asynchronous patterns (accept and queue) for non-immediate operations
Run 1 replica and rely on the HPA to react instantly
Disable rate limiting so all requests reach ACE
Use a single replica with a huge CPU limit
Spikes need protection (rate limits), elasticity (HPA plus node capacity), proactive scaling for known events, and decoupling for work that does not need an immediate answer.
Wrong: HPA and node scaling have lag.
Wrong: a single point of failure, and vertical scaling is limited.
Before the sale, minReplicas goes from 2 to 10; the gateway caps each consumer; orders are queued to MQ and acknowledged with 202.
Known peaks -> pre-scale. Unknown peaks -> autoscale with headroom.
After scaling the DataPower API Gateway from 3 to 5 replicas, rate limits appear inconsistent. What should be checked?
That gateway peering membership includes the new replicas and peering is healthy (the configuration for peers is correct and the peering ports are reachable)
That the portal theme is updated
New replicas must join peering to share rate-limit state. Misconfigured peering leads to per-pod limits.
Correct: verify peering membership and health.
Peering status showed two members missing because of a NetworkPolicy blocking the peering ports.
Why is DataPower considered relatively easy to scale horizontally?
Its request processing is largely stateless, with configuration supplied declaratively and shared state handled through peering, so replicas can be added behind a load balancer
It stores all requests on disk
Stateless processing means replicas are interchangeable. Peering handles the small amount of shared state.
An HPA scales gateway pods from 3 to 6 during peaks.
Which TWO OADP practices are recommended for CP4I backups? (Select TWO.)
Store backups in object storage outside the cluster and region being protected
Test restores into a separate cluster or namespace regularly
Store backups only on the same cluster's local disks
Off-site object storage and regular restore testing are core backup practices. Retention keeps storage under control and meets compliance.
Wrong: unbounded growth or compliance issues.
Backups go to a cross-region S3 bucket with object lock; monthly restore tests run in a DR sandbox.
A restore with OADP into a new cluster succeeds, but CP4I instances do not start because operators are missing. What should the restore procedure include?
Install the required operators (with compatible versions), cert-manager and prerequisites on the target cluster before restoring instance CRs, following the documented CP4I restore order
Restore etcd from the old cluster into the new one
Skip operators because CRs run themselves
CRs need their operators to reconcile them. The documented order is prerequisites and operators first, then configuration and Secrets, then instances and data.
The DR runbook's step 1 installs pinned operator versions through GitOps, then the OADP restore runs.
Restore order matters: platform -> operators -> config -> instances -> data.
Which approach is generally preferred for protecting Event Streams data against regional loss?
Geo-replication (MirrorMaker 2) to a cluster in another region, because broker volume snapshots of a live Kafka cluster are hard to make consistent
Daily snapshots of broker PVs only
Continuous replication gives a low RPO and a consistent, usable target. Volume snapshots of live brokers risk inconsistency and slow recovery.
Critical topics replicate to the DR region with about 2 seconds of lag.
Kafka DR -> replicate, do not snapshot.
Where are API Connect subsystem backups (for example management and portal) typically stored?
In remote storage such as S3-compatible object storage (or SFTP where supported), configured in the subsystem's backup settings

API Connect supports scheduled backups of the management subsystem (its database) and the developer portal to remote storage, typically S3-compatible object storage, or SFTP where supported. The backups must live outside the cluster to be useful for recovery, and the encryption secrets required for restore must be preserved separately.
Correct: remote object storage or SFTP.
Management backs up every 6 hours to an S3 bucket with a 30-day lifecycle.
Configure backups at install time. Do not wait for the first incident.
Which practice BEST validates that a CP4I solution meets its RTO and RPO?
Regular DR exercises (game days) that simulate failures and measure actual recovery time and data loss against objectives
Assuming vendor defaults meet the objectives

Designs and vendor claims are hypotheses until tested. DR exercises (game days) inject realistic failures, measure the actual recovery time and data loss against the stated RTO and RPO, expose gaps in runbooks and dependencies, and train the people who will execute failover in a real incident.
Quarterly game days kill a zone and a region, measuring RTO and RPO per service.

During a regional failover test, everything recovers within RTO, but partner integrations fail for hours because partners had hard-coded IP addresses of the primary region. What design change addresses this?
Expose partner-facing endpoints through stable DNS names (with GSLB) and published egress IP ranges for both regions, and require partners to allow-list both regions
Ask partners to update IPs manually during each disaster
Disable TLS to simplify partner changes
External dependencies must be failover-ready: DNS-based endpoints and pre-agreed IP allow-lists for all regions avoid manual changes during disasters.
Partners now allow-list both regions' egress IPs and use api.partner.example.com with GSLB.
DR includes partners and their configuration.
A StatefulSet pod (for example a Kafka broker) on a failed node is not recreated elsewhere for a long time, while Deployment pods moved quickly. Why?

StatefulSets guarantee at most one pod per identity, so the controller waits until the old pod is confirmed terminated (the node is confirmed down or deleted) before recreating it, to avoid split-brain
For safety, StatefulSet pods on unreachable nodes are not replaced until Kubernetes knows the old pod is gone, for example through node deletion, fencing or out-of-service taints.
Applying the node.kubernetes.io/out-of-service taint after confirming the node was off allowed the broker to restart elsewhere.
StatefulSet failover may need node fencing. Include it in runbooks.
Which probe causes Kubernetes to restart a container that is running but deadlocked?
Liveness probes detect unhealthy containers and trigger restarts. Readiness only removes the pod from traffic.
Wrong: delays other probes during startup.
A hung integration server is restarted after 3 failed liveness checks.
After adding an aggressive liveness probe, a queue manager pod restarts in a loop during heavy recovery after an outage. What should be changed?
Use a startupProbe (or longer initial delay and failure thresholds) so liveness does not kill the pod during legitimate long recovery
Aggressive liveness checks during recovery cause restart loops that prevent recovery from completing.
Correct: protect startup or recovery time.
A startupProbe allowing 15 minutes lets the queue manager finish log replay.
Probes that are too tight turn slow recovery into no recovery.
Which pattern prevents a slow downstream service from exhausting threads in an integration layer and causing cascading failures?
Timeouts plus circuit breakers (and bulkheads), so calls fail fast or degrade gracefully when the dependency is unhealthy
Timeouts bound waiting, circuit breakers stop calls to failing dependencies, and bulkheads isolate resources, all of which limit the blast radius.
The gateway's 5-second timeout and ACE retry with exponential backoff prevented a back-end slowdown from becoming an outage.
Timeouts, retries with backoff, circuit breakers, bulkheads.
After a back end recovers from an outage, it is immediately overwhelmed and fails again. Logs show huge numbers of retries from all clients at once. What is this, and how is it prevented?
A retry storm (thundering herd); prevent it with exponential backoff with jitter, retry limits, rate limiting and queue-based load leveling
Synchronized retries create load spikes. Backoff with jitter spreads them out, and queues smooth the load.
Correct: retry storm and its mitigations.
Adding jittered exponential backoff (1 s, 2 s, 4 s and so on) let the back end recover gradually.
Retry policy design is part of resilience.
How does queue-based load leveling improve resilience?
The queue absorbs bursts so consumers process at a sustainable rate, protecting back ends from overload and decoupling availability
It speeds up the back end
It removes the need for consumers

Queue-based load leveling puts a queue between producers and consumers. Bursts accumulate on the queue instead of overwhelming the back end, consumers process at a sustainable rate, and producers keep working even if consumers are briefly slow or down. The trade-off is added latency during peaks, so monitor queue depth and age.
A batch of 1 million orders is queued, and fulfilment processes 500 per second without crashing.
Spiky load + fragile back end -> put a queue in between.
After a regional failover of MQ, applications in the DR region connect but cannot find some queues that exist in the primary. What was missed?

Queue manager configuration (MQSC, authorities and objects created at runtime) was not kept in sync with the DR queue manager, for example because objects were created manually instead of through declarative configuration
The DR queue manager has too much disk
DR environments drift when changes are made manually in one place. Declarative configuration applied to both sites, or replication of the full queue manager data, prevents this.
Now all MQ objects are defined in Git and applied to both primary and DR through Argo CD.
Configuration drift is a top DR failure cause. Use GitOps.
Why do DR designs usually use a second OpenShift cluster rather than stretching one cluster across distant regions?
etcd and the control plane need low latency between members; long distances cause instability, so independent clusters with replication are used
OpenShift forbids more than one zone
Control plane quorum requires low latency. Regional DR therefore relies on separate clusters and data replication.
Wrong: multi-zone is supported within a region.
Clusters in two regions are kept consistent through GitOps and product-level replication.
Stretch within a metro region at most. Separate clusters across regions.
Pods for an integration runtime use a Vertical Pod Autoscaler in 'Auto' mode and an HPA on CPU at the same time. Scaling behaves erratically. Why?
The VPA changes requests while the HPA uses utilization relative to requests, so the two controllers fight; avoid combining a VPA and an HPA on the same resource metric
Combining a VPA and an HPA on CPU or memory leads to feedback loops. Use the VPA in recommendation mode, or have the HPA use custom metrics.
Switching the VPA to 'Off' (recommendations only) stabilized scaling.
Do not use a VPA and an HPA on the same metric.
How is Event Streams broker capacity scaled out?
Increase the number of brokers in the EventStreams CR, then rebalance partitions (for example with Cruise Control) so the new brokers take load

Adding brokers to an EventStreams instance increases capacity, but existing partitions do not move automatically: new brokers start empty. You must reassign partitions, typically with Cruise Control through a KafkaRebalance resource, so leadership and replicas spread across the enlarged cluster.
Going from 3 to 6 brokers plus a rebalance halved per-broker network load.
Clients see uneven load across ACE replicas behind a Route because each client keeps a long-lived HTTP keep-alive connection. What can help?
Configure the router balancing algorithm (for example leastconn or roundrobin annotations), limit connection reuse on clients, or add more client instances so connections spread
Connection-level balancing pins long-lived connections. Router annotations and client connection management improve distribution.
The annotation haproxy.router.openshift.io/balance: roundrobin improved the spread.
Which statement about synchronous versus asynchronous replication is correct?
Synchronous replication gives RPO near 0 but adds write latency and needs low-latency links; asynchronous replication allows long distances with some potential data loss (RPO greater than 0)
Synchronous replication works well across continents
The replication mode determines RPO and latency impact. That drives HA (synchronous, local) versus DR (asynchronous, remote) designs.
Native HA replicates synchronously within a region; cross-region replication is asynchronous.
Distance and latency drive the choice between sync and async.
Which TWO statements describe a warm standby DR strategy? (Select TWO.)
The DR site runs scaled-down infrastructure and services with data replicated, ready to scale up on failover
RTO is shorter than backup and restore but longer than active/active
The DR site serves full production traffic at all times
Warm standby keeps a reduced environment running and data replicated, so failover needs only scale-up and traffic switching.
Correct: running at reduced scale with replication.
The DR cluster runs one replica of each runtime and scales to production size during failover.
Cold -> pilot light -> warm -> active/active: cost and RTO trade-offs.
How should ACE flows handle a temporarily unavailable back end to avoid losing messages?
Roll back the transaction so the message stays on the input queue for retry (with delays or backout handling), or store it for retry, rather than consuming it and failing
Retry in a tight loop forever without commit
Transactional rollback keeps the message safe. Retry policies and backout queues handle prolonged outages.
During a 10-minute CRM outage, messages remain on the queue and flow once the CRM recovers.
Never acknowledge or consume before successful processing.
A team must design a Kafka cluster across two data centers with RPO 0 for critical topics. Which statement is MOST accurate?

A single stretched cluster with synchronous replication needs low-latency links and a third site (or witness) for quorum, with rack awareness and min.insync.replicas spanning both sites; otherwise two clusters with MirrorMaker 2 cannot give RPO 0
MirrorMaker 2 between two clusters provides RPO 0
Two brokers, one per data center, give RPO 0 and HA
RPO 0 requires synchronous replication within one cluster spanning sites. Quorum and controller placement need a third failure domain. Cross-cluster mirroring is asynchronous.
Correct: stretched cluster, quorum and latency considerations.
Wrong: no quorum and insufficient replicas.
Wrong: possible with the right design.
Three sites within 5 ms: two main data centers with brokers and a small third site for quorum.
RPO 0 across sites = synchronous + quorum (3 sites) + low latency.
An application needs HA messaging but connects in bindings mode (local) on a VM today. What must change when moving to MQ Native HA on OpenShift?
The application must connect as a client over the network (with reconnect options), because bindings mode requires running on the same host as the queue manager
Nothing; bindings mode works across pods
The application must run inside the queue manager pod
Containerized queue managers are reached over the network. Client mode with auto-reconnect is the standard for HA queue managers on Kubernetes.
Correct: switch to client mode with reconnect.
The JMS application switches from bindings to client mode with a CCDT and the reconnect option.
What is the benefit of running at least two replicas of a stateless integration component?
A single pod failure or node drain does not cause an outage
It removes the need for monitoring

With one replica, any pod crash, node failure or node drain for maintenance takes the service down until a replacement starts, which can take minutes. With at least two replicas (plus a PodDisruptionBudget and spreading), one instance can fail or be drained while the other keeps serving.
Correct: no single point of failure.
With 2 replicas plus a PDB, node upgrades proceed with no downtime.
Two replicas minimum for anything that matters.
Which design BEST avoids a single point of failure in an end-to-end integration path: Client -> Gateway -> ACE -> MQ -> Back end?
Redundancy at every tier: multiple gateway replicas, multiple ACE replicas, Native HA queue managers, a back end with HA, zone spreading and resilient dependencies (DNS, identity, certificates)
A large single instance for each tier
The path is only as available as its weakest component, so every tier and shared dependency needs redundancy.
Wrong: other tiers remain single points of failure.
Wrong: other tiers remain single points of failure.
Availability analysis multiplies each tier's availability; the weakest link determines the overall SLA.
Overall availability = product of tier availabilities.
Which OpenShift operator provides KEDA-based event-driven autoscaling (for example on queue depth or Kafka lag)?
The Custom Metrics Autoscaler Operator, based on KEDA, scales workloads based on external metrics such as Kafka lag, Prometheus queries or MQ depth.
A ScaledObject scales MQ consumers when queue depth exceeds 1,000.
Event-driven scaling on OpenShift = Custom Metrics Autoscaler (KEDA).
A KEDA ScaledObject scales consumers to zero during quiet periods, but the first messages after idle wait several minutes. Why, and what can be done?

Scale-from-zero requires the trigger to detect work, start pods and complete their startup (image pull, connections); set minReplicaCount to 1 for latency-sensitive flows, or reduce the polling interval and startup time
Scale-to-zero saves resources but adds cold-start latency. Latency-sensitive services should keep a warm minimum.
Setting minReplicaCount to 1 for the payments consumer removed the 3-minute first-message delay.
Scale to zero = cost saving + cold-start latency.
A CP4I estate must be recoverable after ransomware encrypts the cluster and its storage. Which backup strategy is MOST appropriate?

Immutable, off-site backups (object lock or WORM) with separate credentials, combined with configuration in Git (protected separately), product-level data backups, and tested clean-room restore procedures
Snapshots on the same storage array
Backups stored in the same cluster with the same admin credentials
Ransomware can corrupt replicas and reachable backups. Immutable, isolated backups with separate access, plus rehearsed restores into a clean environment, are essential.
Backups go to an object-locked bucket in a separate account; a quarterly clean-room restore is performed.
Replication does not equal backup. Corruption replicates too.
What happens when the leader replica of a Kafka partition fails?
An in-sync follower is elected as the new leader, and clients redirect requests to it after refreshing metadata

Every partition has one leader. If the leader's broker fails, the controller elects a new leader from the in-sync replicas (ISR). Producers and consumers receive errors briefly, refresh their metadata, and continue against the new leader. Clean election requires at least one in-sync replica to survive.
Correct: leader election from the ISR.
Broker 1 crashes; partitions led by it fail over to brokers 2 and 3 within seconds.
An ISR is needed for clean leader election.
A partition has no in-sync replicas after a double failure, and unclean.leader.election.enable is false. The partition stays offline. What is the trade-off of enabling unclean leader election?
It restores availability by electing an out-of-sync replica, but can lose committed data; for critical topics, keep it disabled and recover the in-sync replica

If no in-sync replica survives, Kafka can only restore availability by electing an out-of-sync replica (unclean leader election). That replica may lack recently acknowledged records, so they are lost. Keep unclean election disabled for critical topics and recover an in-sync replica instead; enable it only where availability matters more than completeness.
For a metrics topic, availability matters more, so unclean election is enabled; for payments, it is disabled.
Consistency versus availability, per topic criticality.
What is a simple prerequisite for running more than one replica of an ACE integration runtime that serves HTTP?
The flows must not rely on local in-pod state between requests (statelessness), because requests are balanced across replicas
Each replica needs its own BAR file
Replicas must run on control plane nodes
With several replicas, consecutive requests can hit different pods, so flows must be stateless or use shared external state.
Wrong: the same BAR is used.
A session token cache was moved from memory to an external cache before scaling to 3 replicas.
Why should failback (returning to the primary site) be planned and tested as carefully as failover?
Failback involves re-synchronizing data written in the DR site back to the primary and switching traffic again, which can cause data loss or conflicts if improvised
Failback is automatic in every product
Failback only affects the Platform UI
Data created during DR must be replicated back before switching. Improvised failback risks losing transactions or creating split-brain.
The runbook reverses the replication direction, verifies lag is zero, then switches traffic back.
DR = failover + operating in DR + failback.
